title: Financial statements and equity valuation for advisers
objectives: Use P/E, P/B, ROE and dividend yield to explain a stock to a client.
Recognise the limits of ratio-based advice.
body_md:
## Ratios an adviser should explain simply

| Ratio | Formula | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| **EPS** | Profit after tax ÷ shares | Profit per share |
| **P/E** | Price ÷ EPS | Years of earnings paid for |
| **P/B** | Price ÷ book value per share | Useful for banks |
| **ROE** | PAT ÷ shareholders' equity | Quality of profit on owners' money |
| **Dividend yield** | Dividend ÷ price | Cash return |
| **PEG** | P/E ÷ growth rate | Growth-adjusted P/E |

## Using them

- Compare with **peers and history**, not with a single number.
- A low P/E can signal a **value trap**; a high P/E needs high growth to justify it.
- Prefer companies with **steady ROE, modest debt and cash backing profits**.

## Worked example

Price ₹300, EPS ₹15: **P/E = 20**. Dividend ₹6: yield 2%. ROE 18% with falling debt supports a premium over a 12% ROE peer.

## For mutual fund clients

Use a fund's **portfolio P/E and P/B** to describe whether it leans to value or growth.

## Limits

Ratios use past data. They guide a conversation; they are not a recommendation on their own.

> **Exam tip:** P/E = price ÷ EPS. Use banks' P/B with ROE.
example: Price ₹300 and EPS ₹15 give a P/E of 20. A peer at P/E 14 with the same growth looks cheaper, so ask why before concluding.
say: Compared with its peers, this stock is priced richer; here is why that may be fair.
Past ratios do not predict future results.
never: A low P/E always means a bargain.
